title: The Upgrade of Minescout Life and Its Web Presence — Part 1: The Site
summary: A behind-the-scenes look at how MineScout Life went from a tangled mess of vanilla JS and Firebase to a clean, fast React app — told through every bug, fix, and version along the way.
content:
The Problem With v3

MineScout Life v3 worked. Mostly. If you didn't look too closely at the code, or try to edit it, or open it on a phone, or add a new post without knowing exactly where to poke in the Firebase console. It was one of those sites that had been built incrementally — a feature added here, a fix patched there — until the whole thing was a single 27,000-byte index.html file with six script tags at the bottom, a 31,000-byte CSS file, Firebase Realtime Database holding every post, and a collection of separate HTML files for each article that all had their own copies of the header, footer, and styles baked in.

The symptoms were obvious once you started listing them. The mobile layout broke in multiple places — stat cards overflowed, the sidebar crushed itself, post cards clipped their content. Load times were slow because every page visit had to pull Firebase, authenticate, fetch posts, and then render them one by one. Adding a new post meant going into the Firebase console, writing a JSON object by hand, getting the timestamp right, and hoping you didn't typo a field name. Editing an existing post meant finding the right HTML file, opening it, hunting through hundreds of lines of copy-pasted markup, making the change, and saving — with no preview and no safety net. And the codebase itself was split across auth.js, loader.js, homepage.js, features.js, data.js, sidebar.js, and firebase-config.js, all loading independently and depending on each other in ways that weren't documented anywhere.

It was time to start over.

The Starting Point

The decision was to rebuild in React using Vite — fast builds, instant hot reload, proper component structure, and a dev experience that works perfectly inside code-server. Firebase would be cut entirely. Posts would live as plain JSON files on the server, readable by anyone and editable without a database account. The admin panel would live inside the React app itself, protected by a simple session password. And every one of the existing 30-something HTML posts would be migrated into the new system with their real content, real dates, and real images intact.

The old site's file structure told the whole story of how it had grown organically: assests/ (yes, with the typo — kept intentionally to avoid breaking image paths), posts/tech/, posts/updates/, posts/puppy/, archives/ full of month-by-month HTML files that were all identical placeholder shells, a projects/ folder with standalone HTML apps like GeoMaster and the Vigenere cipher, and a software stuff/ folder with two text files. The zip file alone was 563MB — mostly because it contained two full desktop app installers sitting in posts/updates/app stuff/.

v1 — Getting the Foundation Right

The first version scaffolded the Vite React project and got the core architecture working. Firebase was replaced with a fetchPosts() function that loads /public/posts/manifest.json — a flat array of post metadata that the homepage uses to render the timeline. Individual post bodies live in separate JSON files at /public/posts/[id].json, fetched only when you click through to read an article. This meant the homepage loads fast (one small JSON file) and post content only loads when you need it.

The homepage was rebuilt with all its original features: animated stat counters, category filter cards, the 90-day contribution heatmap, the AI reflection sidebar module that calls the existing Cloudflare Worker, the Now Building section, the year-grouped timeline, and the dark/light theme toggle using localStorage. Auth was replaced with a simple sessionStorage password check — enter the right password at /login, get admin access for the session, close the tab and it resets.

It built cleanly in under two seconds. But there were immediate problems. Every post card linked to the old /posts/tech/ai-comparison.html paths — React Router was intercepting those and returning 404s. There was no way to write actual article body content. And images had no defined home in the new structure.

v2 — The Migration and the Editor

This was the biggest version. The goal was to get every existing post into the new system with full content, and to build a real admin panel for writing new ones.

A Python migration script read every HTML file in posts/tech/, posts/updates/, posts/puppy/, and posts/beta/, extracted the article content using regex against the <article> tag, stripped out the old site's header and footer markup, pulled the real title from the <h1>, pulled the date from the post-meta paragraph, and grabbed the hero image path. Each post was written to its own JSON file and an entry added to manifest.json. 30 posts migrated in one run.

A new /post/:id route was added to React Router that fetches the full post JSON and renders the content as raw HTML using dangerouslySetInnerHTML — which is fine here since all the content comes from your own files, not user input. A Tiptap rich text editor landed in the admin panel for writing new posts. The Vite dev server got a custom plugin that added /api/save-post and /api/delete-post endpoints — these write directly to the public/posts/ folder and update manifest.json in real time, so publishing a post from the browser instantly makes it live on the site.

Two problems carried over into the next version: icons were broken everywhere, and several post dates were wrong.

v3 — Design Overhaul, Icons Fixed, HTML Editor

The purple dashboard aesthetic of v3 was replaced entirely. The new design is editorial — warm paper tones (#faf8f5 in light mode, #16140f in dark), Lora serif for headings, Inter for body text, a forest green accent palette. Post cards feel more like clippings than dashboard widgets. The sidebar is quieter. The hero text uses italic serif for the word "Builder." — a small thing that makes a big difference.

The icon problem turned out to be simple once diagnosed: every migrated post used Google Material Symbols Rounded — check_circle, workspace_premium, arrow_back, and others — via the material-symbols-rounded CSS class. The old site loaded the font in each HTML file's <head>. The new React app didn't load it at all, so every icon rendered as its raw text name. One line added to index.html fixed all of them across every post at once.

The Tiptap rich text editor was swapped for a plain HTML textarea. The reason: Tiptap adds a lot of complexity and produces its own HTML that sometimes differs from what you'd write by hand. Since you were already comfortable with HTML from building the original posts, a raw editor with a live preview toggle was cleaner and gave more control — full tables, custom inline styles, anything valid HTML supports.

v4 — Year Filtering and the Real Post Count

A proper audit of the source zip revealed the actual post count was 32, not 30. Two posts had been missed entirely in the first migration: the GPT Number Guessing Game and The Cuboid Oracle (a Gemini-built number game). Both had no dates in their HTML — they were assigned October 2025 dates. A third post, the Gemini Fast vs GPT-4o image comparison, had a literal [INSERT DATE] placeholder — assigned November 1, 2025.

The bigger date problem was the six ai-post-test-* articles. Their HTML had Posted 8/19/2025 — but the migration script couldn't parse that format and silently fell back to a random timestamp, which ended up in 2024. All six were corrected to August 19, 2025.

The homepage was updated to show only the current year by default — since you're actively posting in 2026, showing 2025 posts immediately would bury the recent stuff. Year tabs appear above the timeline (2026, 2025, 2024...) so you can jump to any year in one click. The archive links in the sidebar became clickable filters that do the same thing. A "Show all years" option lets you see everything at once.

Going Live

Deployment ended up simpler than expected. The server already runs nginx with a config that handles several domains. Rather than building to a static dist/ folder and copying files, the nginx config for life.minescout.net was updated to proxy all traffic to Vite's dev server running on port 3000. PM2 keeps the dev server alive permanently — surviving tab closes, terminal sessions ending, and server reboots. The images folder (assests/, typo and all) lives in public/ so Vite includes it in every build automatically.

The admin panel's save and delete endpoints work in dev mode, which is exactly what's running in production. So writing a post, publishing it, and seeing it live on the timeline is a single action with no deploy step in between.

What the New Stack Actually Is

For anyone curious: Vite 8 + React 19, React Router v7 for client-side navigation, plain CSS custom properties for theming (no Tailwind, no CSS-in-JS), Lora + Inter from Google Fonts, Material Symbols Rounded for icons, a custom Vite server plugin for the post API, PM2 for process management, and nginx as the reverse proxy. No Firebase. No external database. No build pipeline beyond npm run dev. Total JS bundle: 260kb gzipped to 82kb. CSS: 18kb gzipped to 4kb. Build time: under 200ms.

The post system is about as simple as it gets: a JSON file per post, a manifest JSON for the homepage to read, and a browser-based admin to write and manage them. The whole thing lives in ~/workspace/life.minescout.net/ on the server, editable directly in code-server, updating live on every save.

What's Next

Part 2 will cover the rest of the MineScout web presence — minescout.net, the projects, the beta mainframe, and what's being planned for v4.1 of this site. The features request board, better archive pages, and possibly a proper search are all on the list.

For now: the site is faster, the code is maintainable, adding a post takes two minutes instead of fifteen, and it works on mobile. That's the whole win.

This post was written with the help of Claude Sonnet 4.6 — the AI assistant that handled the architecture decisions, wrote the migration scripts, rebuilt every component, debugged the icon rendering, fixed the dates, and produced somewhere around 1,200 lines of CSS across five versions of this rebuild. The ideas, the content, and the direction are mine. The heavy code lifting was a collaboration. That felt worth documenting.
